name: Rafael Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you say stays confidential. Describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael Petrov, 58, and I took a vocational certificate after years in building plumbing. Now I'm a junior lineworker at the electricity company, building and repairing lines under Ed's eye; I like the clear result, but a tight cable joint still catches the plumbing habits in my hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do when those habits show up?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I stop and ask Ed to look. He showed me a sleeve gap at the mill tap last week, and I wrote the angle in my manual for next time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot a quicker work ticket would be pleasant, but someone still has to bring the light back. The cable doesn't care whether the writing came from a person or a program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't mind that future at all. I changed from building plumbing to line work at 55, and I'm still junior; good pay and ten months of bills saved let me take the time to learn it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll continue the assigned line repairs with my crew lead watching the tricky connections. In the first year I'd keep paying our normal savings amount and use the approved AI note tool now and then, after my work is safely finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled, and grateful that learning a new trade at my age hasn't been wasted. My wife Marta and I have grown children, so the house is quieter than it used to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which connection needs the most watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tap near the mill has a tight angle, and my crew lead Ed checks my sleeve before the cover goes back. I still catch myself reaching as if it were plumbing pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you ask the note tool to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only shorten a long account of what we already did. It can't approve an isolation; Ed and the meter reading handle that.

say: I'd welcome **shorter work tickets** after a long repair call at the mill.
I'd say **restoring power** still takes field workers.
think: My **late trade change** needs more supervised practice.
Our **ten-month reserve** and good pay make minor automation comfortable.
do: Continue **assigned repairs** while Ed checks difficult connections.
Use the **approved note tool** occasionally after repairs and maintain normal savings deposits.
feel: **Settled** and glad the late trade change has time to mature.
S0.quote: The cable doesn't care whether the writing came from a person or a program.
fieldNote: Rafael's **plumbing habits** still surface at tight cable joints, so he accepts Ed's supervision rather than overstating his skill.
His **occasional AI use** stays after the repair, within a household supported by strong savings and higher pay.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs with Ed checking difficult cable joints
Use the approved AI note tool after completed repair calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers to test the new booking system with the dispatchers before reducing their shifts. The crew might receive clearer orders, but a missing street name can waste a whole morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own line repairs should continue for now, but Marta does payroll for a small manufacturer, and checking wages is exactly the sort of thinking work the card describes. Our savings would carry us for a while, yet her hours could go before mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask Ed to show me the approved fault map once the dispatchers have tried it. During the first year Marta and I would move her bonus into the emergency account instead of booking the family reunion trip, until we know whether her payroll role survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for her and for the dispatchers. I'll learn a system that has passed a real trial, but I won't pretend a better map replaces local judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could a map miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The service lane to the mill is closed after heavy rain even when the main road is open. Our dispatcher knows where the gate key is. A map can draw a road through water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the trip change to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children we're postponing the reunion, not asking them to pay for it. They have their own bills, and we can visit separately later.

say: I'd ask **dispatchers** to test booking software before their shifts change.
I'd welcome **clearer orders** if local access knowledge remains.
think: My **line repairs** continue for now, but Marta's payroll hours could shrink.
Our **savings** buy time without replacing a lost second wage.
do: Learn the **approved fault map** after dispatchers finish real-call trials.
Move Marta's **bonus to emergency savings** and postpone the reunion while her role is uncertain.
feel: **Uneasy** for Marta and dispatch staff, open to a tested map.
S1.quote: A map can draw a road through water.
fieldNote: Rafael's **household risk** comes early through Marta's payroll work, while his physical repairs remain for now.
He will **increase savings** with an actual bonus and delay a reunion, rather than expecting grown children to pay.

steps.text: Learn the approved fault map after dispatchers test it on real calls
Transfer Marta’s bonus to emergency savings while payroll hours are uncertain
Postpone the family reunion trip until Marta’s payroll role is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the thinking AI in 2028 may write the plan, but the machine that can actually mend a line comes around 2031. We need a clear apprenticeship path for the people whose jobs shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031 I may still need the wage, especially if Marta's payroll work has already changed. Ten months saved is a good buffer, and there are several utilities nearby, but I can't assume each one wants a junior worker my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the training office for the requirements of its inspection apprenticeship and get a written retirement estimate. In 2029 I'd enroll if the apprenticeship is paid; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for inspection openings locally and keep paid repair shifts until I have an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, but the buffer gives us breathing room to make calls. I don't want an allowance for doing nothing; I want a path to useful paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta say about a new apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Marta would want the wages and hours written down before I signed. Our grown son might tell me where vacancies are, but he has his own family to support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection be safe from thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, its reports could be done by the system too. I'd ask what part of the job still needs a human inspection and how long the employer expects to pay for it.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning AI** from 2031 repair robots.
I'd call for a **paid apprenticeship** before field posts shrink.
think: At **63**, I may need wages after Marta's payroll hours change.
Nearby utilities are **options**, not guaranteed hires for an older junior.
do: Check **inspection apprenticeship requirements** and request a retirement estimate now.
Enroll if **paid in 2029**, then apply for real inspection openings when robots arrive.
feel: **Worried**, with savings enough to make careful calls.
S2.quote: I want a path to useful paid work.
fieldNote: Rafael's **apprenticeship choice** is conditional on pay and an employer's explanation of what human inspection still involves.
He separates **thinking work in 2028** from field repair robots in 2031, while Marta's payroll income adds earlier pressure.

steps.text: Enroll in a paid inspection apprenticeship in 2029 if offered
Apply for local inspection openings when field robots arrive
Keep paid repair shifts until an actual offer arrives
Request a written retirement estimate before changing work plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot five years should allow a proper trial and proper training, rather than a hurried deal. Thinking AI reaches plans in 2031 and field robots reach repairs around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 66 when robots can take repair calls, so retirement might be possible, but Marta's payroll income may already be lower. I'd rather use real figures than tell myself the savings will last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask for retirement forecasts for both of us and talk with Ed about paid work checking robot repairs. In 2032 I'd take the company's inspection course if it is paid and recognised; in 2034 I'd choose retirement if our budget works, or apply for posted inspection shifts if it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to plan than in the fast picture. I still feel a pull between wanting to finish my working years well and not gambling the house budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small home loan, medicine, and a low estimate for Marta's payroll hours. We wouldn't count a bonus until it was actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you keep climbing at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if my health holds and the company still has safe crew shifts. I won't write that into the plan as a certainty.

say: I'd ask for **proper field trials** and paid training before 2034 robots.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from later physical repairs.
think: Retirement at **66** may work only with Marta's lower-income case.
I won't treat **savings** or future crew shifts as permanent income.
do: Get **both retirement forecasts** and ask Ed about paid robot-repair checks.
Take a **paid recognised course** in 2032 if offered, then retire or apply for posted inspection shifts in 2034.
feel: **More able to plan**, while protective of the house budget.
S3.quote: We wouldn't count a bonus until it was actually paid.
fieldNote: Rafael's **2034 retirement decision** includes a low case for Marta's payroll hours and excludes unpaid bonuses.
The **inspection course** must be paid and recognised, and he only applies to a real vacancy if retirement falls short.

steps.text: Compare both written retirement forecasts with the home loan and medicine
Take the paid recognised inspection course in 2032 if offered
Apply for posted inspection shifts in 2034 if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger crew to learn how to test a line before learning how to supervise a machine. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, then repair robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to be retired from climbing before 71 if the forecasts cover us. Marta's payroll job might change in 2036, so I would check that risk each year instead of assuming her current pay continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid line shifts and teach the newest trainee how to check the mill tap with Ed watching. In 2037 Marta and I would set a retirement date if our low-income budget covers bills; in 2039 I'd leave the trainee my annotated manual, even if I'm retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my near-term wages and grateful to have time to pass on what I've learned. A late apprentice can still be useful to the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is written by the mill tap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My note says to check the sleeve from below before closing the cover, because the angle hides a small gap. Ed caught mine once, and a new trainee should not repeat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the budget does not cover retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid crew work if it's available and look at a real inspection opening. We could also postpone the date, but I wouldn't ask our children to carry our costs.

say: I'd ask trainees to learn **line testing** before supervising machines.
I'd explain **2039 robots** reach repairs when I'll be 71.
think: I may retire before **71** if both forecasts cover the bills.
Marta's **payroll income** could change in 2036 and needs annual review.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and teach the mill tap check with Ed present.
Set a **2037 retirement date** if the low-income budget works; leave an annotated manual in 2039.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages and keen to pass on practical skill.
S4.quote: A late apprentice can still be useful to the next one.
fieldNote: Rafael's longer runway gives him a **teaching role**, but he does not treat that role as protected paid work after robots.
His **retirement date** remains conditional on Marta's payroll income and a low-income household budget.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and teach the mill tap check under Ed
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if low-income figures cover bills
Apply for a real inspection opening if retirement figures fall short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Marta's payroll work could shrink before repair robots arrive in 2031. A paid inspection apprenticeship, real postings, clear staffing notice and reliable household income figures would help us keep working and plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a new certificate leads to a paid shift, not just a ceremony. I'd rather be told the truth while I still have time to apply elsewhere.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be told the truth while I still have time to apply elsewhere.
portrait: Rafael is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who moved from building plumbing and still takes Ed's help with tight cable joints.
His **ten-month reserve** provide room, while Marta's payroll job exposes their income to thinking AI first.
He uses **AI occasionally** for completed repair notes and adopts field tools after experienced staff test them.
The **2031 robot arrival** worries him because he may still need wages and a certificate may not bring an inspection job.
Longer warning lets him **check retirement income**, take paid training if offered and teach a specific cable check to trainees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Rafael most because Marta's payroll wages may shrink before field robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **paid inspection apprenticeship**, real job postings, clear notice and reliable household income figures.
